resources.string: More > Routines lists the routines your server keeps, the ones made in the Roborock app, and runs one with a tap.
Both now send the spot you drew or tapped in the robot's own coordinates, so the robot goes where you meant.
Pick a type such as Kitchen or Bedroom for a room, or give it a name of your own.
Set a schedule to any minute, shown in your phone's clock style. If the robot refuses a schedule, the app now says so.
On newer robots, Settings > Beta features switches options such as FlexiArm and gap deep clean. Only options your robot reports are shown.

A zoomed map now reaches the edge of the screen and keeps its zoom while the robot cleans. After a floor switch the right map appears once the robot has loaded it. Rooms can be renamed on robots with an empty room table, dock settings follow what each dock supports, the built-in water tank can be emptied through the dock, and the back button returns to the settings list. The sign-in screen is available in German.
Choose Per room in the cleaning mode to give every room its own suction, water and route, for example mopping the kitchen and only vacuuming the bedroom.
Rooms you pick are cleaned in the order you tap them. More > Rooms > Default cleaning order sets the order for a clean without picked rooms.
On robots that have it, SmartPlan lets the robot choose suction, water and route for each room.
Settings > Notifications can tell you when a robot gets stuck, finishes cleaning, or its dock needs attention.

The app connects faster when it starts and after the screen was off, and no longer shows a robot as online when it is not. Map editing and map switching work on older robots, and a robot that never used the official app can save its first map.
Tap the pencil on the map to draw no-go zones, invisible walls, carpets and thresholds, split and merge rooms, and set floor types.
More > Maps renames and deletes maps, and sends the robot out to map the home again, for example after moving the dock.
Keep a map for each floor, switch between them with the picker on the map, or let the robot recognise the floor by itself.
Mapping runs show as Mapping, round carpets keep their shape, and the cleaned area no longer flickers while the map changes.
Local control for your robot vacuum
LocalRock runs entirely on your own network. Three things to know before you start.
LocalRock talks to a self-hosted LocalRock server. Until that is running on your network, the app has nothing to control.
The email and login code come from your own server setup — not a new cloud account.
Your phone and the server have to be able to reach each other locally.
LocalRock is an independent community project, not affiliated with or endorsed by Roborock.
LocalRock talks only to the LocalRock server running on your own network. Enter its address to continue.
Use the server root, including the port. Don't add /admin.
No vacuums are available for onboarding yet. Finish the cloud import / fetch-data step on the server first.
Load and select a vacuum to onboard first
Server did not return a session id
Wi-Fi sent. Waiting for the vacuum to reach the server…
Vacuum connected and its public key was recovered. It should now appear in your device list.
The vacuum reached the server, but its public key was never recovered, so it will appear in the list with no data. Factory-reset the vacuum and run onboarding again, keeping it next to the dock.
The server reported an identity conflict — this vacuum is already registered under different credentials. Remove it on the server, then retry.
The server has the vacuum's public key, but the vacuum is not connected yet. Run Add vacuum once more to finish.
The vacuum reached the server, which does not have its public key yet. That usually takes two or three rounds: run Add vacuum again.

Wi-Fi was sent, but the vacuum hasn't reported to the server within the wait window. Keep it powered near the dock, it can take a few minutes. If it never shows up, check that the vacuum can reach the server from its network. Some older models also reject the server's certificate without any error and need one from another authority (see the server's tested vacuums list).
Put the robot in pairing mode, then connect it to your home Wi-Fi.
After the robot joins your network, it will appear in the device list. This can take around 30 seconds.
Use the network your robot should join.
For remote viewing: a hostname of at most 14 characters that reaches your server on 443. Leave empty to send the country code.
Also use as the robot's server name
Needed for remote viewing on a Saros 20 or Qrevo MaxV. The robot then reaches the server as api-%1$s, so that name must reach it too.
Sign in to your server's admin panel and pick the vacuum to onboard. It must already be imported on the server (cloud fetch-data step).
Enter Wi-Fi details and start pairing.
Waiting for the robot to respond…
Waiting for the robot to join your network…
You'll need to log in again with an email code to control your vacuums.
Add your first vacuum, or pull down to check the server again.

Draw rooms with straight walls from the robot's floor plan, as the Roborock app does. Off shows the robot's own map pixels.
The address of your self-hosted LocalRock server on your network.
Control vacuums locally through your own server. Not affiliated with, endorsed by, or connected to Roborock. "Roborock" is a trademark of its owner.
LocalRock stands on the shoulders of open-source work. With thanks to:
And to the reverse-engineering community — especially the python-roborock project — whose protocol work made local control possible.
Allow notifications for LocalRock in your phone's settings to get robot alerts.
Tells you when a robot gets stuck, finishes cleaning, or its dock needs attention.
Clean water empty, dirty water full, dust bag missing.
Keeps the connection to your server open so alerts arrive while the app is closed. Android shows one permanent notification while this is on.
While a clean runs, the background notification shows what the robot is doing, which room it is in, and how far along it is.
Alerts come straight from your own server, so they only arrive while your phone can reach it: on your home Wi-Fi or through your VPN.
Alerts arrive while LocalRock is open. iOS does not let an app keep a connection to your own server open in the background, and LocalRock does not send anything through Apple's push service.
The robot has no saved map yet. Map edits need a saved map.
The robot stores at most %1$d zone and wall points. Remove one first.
Checking the robot's saved maps. You can edit now; saving waits for this.
The robot will keep exactly these: %1$s. Anything removed here is removed from the robot.
Where you deleted a carpet the robot found, it stops detecting carpet.

Floor type sent. This robot's map doesn't report floor types, so LocalRock can't confirm it.

The robot divides the room along the line you drew. The line must cross the room from wall to wall. Both parts get new room numbers, so give them names afterwards and check any schedules that include this room.
Room split. The robot's map shows the new rooms. Name them from the room list.
%1$s and %2$s become one room. They must be next to each other, or the robot refuses. The merged room may lose its name, and schedules that include either room may need updating.
Rooms merged. The robot's map shows one room.
Found by the robot. Deleting it turns carpet detection off in this area.
